idiom_name: abstract base class with protected primitives and an abstract sandbox method (ControllerBase shape)
implementation_notes: C# supplies the whole structure with keywords: an abstract base class, protected non-virtual primitives, protected abstract or protected virtual members for the sandbox method, and override plus sealed override to control further derivation; protected internal widens a primitive to the assembly only when a sibling assembly has to extend the family. ASP.NET Core's ControllerBase is the everyday real-world form - a controller subclass composes actions from the provided operations Ok(), NotFound(), BadRequest(), User and ModelState while the framework owns routing and the response - and System.IO.Stream shows the narrower template-method-flavoured cousin where the base implements the array operations over the required Read/Write. What replaces the classic structure is composition with a registered services value when the behaviours share no state; keep the abstract base when the family shares stored state or lifecycle.
pitfalls: The access modifier is the sandbox wall: a primitive declared public (or left at the default) becomes part of the public surface, and protected internal lets every type in the assembly - including tests and unrelated helpers - call it.

Class members are non-virtual by default, so a primitive that was meant to stay fixed is safe, but one that was meant to be overridden and is not marked virtual silently hides a same-name member in a derived class.

Any derived class can override a virtual sandbox method, and a mocking framework that intercepts virtual members can too; seal the behaviours (and intermediate types) when the family must not be extended further.
Calling Activate() from the base constructor runs before the derived class's field initialisers, so behaviour code sees uninitialised state.
